triggers: how do I install InterGenOS
how do I run the installer
how do I install the system to disk
how to use Forge
what's the installer called
how do I reinstall or recover
answer:
InterGenOS is installed with **Forge**, the built-in installer. Boot the InterGenOS ISO (USB or DVD); from the boot menu you can run the **live** session to try it, or launch **Forge** to install. Forge walks you through disk selection, optional full-disk encryption, your user account, and (optionally) Secure Boot — then writes and signs the boot chain for your machine.

For repair, boot the same ISO and use the live session's recovery tools (mount your install, `chroot` in, fix, reboot). Forge can also re-run an install over an existing one.

is my disk encrypted

answer:
Full-disk encryption uses **LUKS** and is set up **during the Forge install** — tick the encryption option and choose a passphrase. Once installed, the disk is unlocked by that passphrase at boot, before the system starts.

It has to be chosen at install time because it encrypts the whole root filesystem; you can't retro-fit it onto an unencrypted install without reinstalling. To check whether a disk is encrypted, `lsblk` shows a `crypt` layer over the partition. Manage the LUKS volume (e.g. add a recovery key) with `cryptsetup`.

triggers: how do I enable secure boot
how does secure boot work on InterGenOS
what is MOK enrollment
how do I check if secure boot is on
do I need to enroll a key
how do I turn on secure boot and MOK
answer:
On InterGenOS, Secure Boot is **OFF by default and optional** — the boot chain (shim → GRUB → signed kernel image) is signed and verifiable either way, and the kernel runs in lockdown=integrity regardless. You don't have to enable Secure Boot, and on a default install no key enrollment is required.

If you *want* firmware-enforced Secure Boot: enable it in your firmware setup, then on the next reboot **MokManager** prompts you to enroll InterGenOS's Machine Owner Key (MOK) — accept it once. Forge generates that per-machine MOK during install; enrolling it only matters when Secure Boot is on (and for trusting your own out-of-tree/DKMS modules under enforcement).

Check the current state:

```
mokutil --sb-state        # SecureBoot enabled / disabled
```

triggers: how does package signing work
how do I know my packages are trusted
how does InterGenOS verify packages
what's the signing model
how do I verify the package index is genuine
how do I check a package hasn't been tampered with
answer:
Every InterGenOS package index is signed by the project's **operator master key**, and `pkm` verifies that signature against the keyring shipped on your system before it trusts any index it downloads — a forged or modified index is rejected. The master key's fingerprint is pinned (`5597 A3E0 587B 2530 06D0  DD7B 8C50 8261 8208 3050`).

To check that your installed files still match what was installed (tamper / corruption check), use:

```
pkm verify            # re-hash every installed package's files
```

This is the package-integrity counterpart to the signed *index*: signing proves the index is genuine; `pkm verify` proves your on-disk files haven't changed since install.

I run **fully locally** on your machine and I'm offline by design — I don't browse the web or pull live feeds, so I can't give you real-time facts like today's stock prices, news headlines, or the current weather.
